Pipetting. A fundamental laboratory technique used to measure and transfer a precise volume of liquid. It utilizes a device called a pipette, and is widely used across chemistry, biology, molecular biology, and clinical medicine to handle liquid reagents, prepare dilutions, and run assays.

Several types of pipettes serve different purposes. Volumetric pipettes, also called bulb pipettes, transfer a single, highly accurate volume of liquid, characterized by a large central bulb and a single etched calibration line. Graduated pipettes such as Mohr or serological pipettes measure variable volumes, with serological pipettes designed to be blown out to deliver their full volume. Micropipettes, which are piston-driven air displacement pipettes, handle microliter-scale volumes ranging from one to one thousand microliters and require disposable plastic tips to prevent sample cross-contamination. Pasteur pipettes are uncalibrated glass or plastic droppers used for simple transfers where quantitative accuracy is not required.

Achieving accuracy requires specific technical steps. Pre-wetting the pipette tip is essential, as is holding the pipette vertically during aspiration and dispensing at a forty-five degree angle with the tip touching the receiving vessel's wall. Micropipettes are calibrated gravimetrically by measuring the mass of purified water they dispense, using the temperature-dependent density of water. Classic volumetric and Pasteur pipettes are made of borosilicate glass, which is chemically inert and thermal-shock resistant. A volumetric pipette is used to deliver the exact volume of analyte into the titration flask during quantitative analysis.
